Question: In triangle \(ABC\) the medians \(AM\) and \(CN\) to sides \(BC\) and \(AB,\) respectively, intersect in point \(O.\) \(P\) is the midpoint of side \(AC,\) and \(MP\) intersects \(CN\) in \(Q.\) If the area of triangle \(OMQ\) is \(n,\) then the area of triangle \(ABC\) is:
Solution:
Method 1: Use median, midsegment, and common-height ratios

The useful comparison is between triangles \(OMQ\) and \(CMN\): their bases \(OQ\) and \(CN\) lie on the same line, and both have vertex \(M\). Their area ratio is therefore their base ratio.

Since \(M\) and \(P\) are the midpoints of \(CB\) and \(CA\), the midsegment theorem gives \(MP\parallel AB\). Thus \(MQ\parallel BN\), making triangles \(CMQ\) and \(CBN\) similar. Consequently,
\[
\frac{CQ}{CN}=\frac{CM}{CB}=\frac12.
\]
The intersection \(O\) of the medians is the centroid, which divides each median in a \(2:1\) ratio from its vertex. Hence \(CO=2CN/3\). Along \(CN\), the order is \(C,Q,O,N\), so
\[
OQ=\left(\frac23-\frac12\right)CN=\frac16CN.
\]
Write \([XYZ]\) for the area of triangle \(XYZ\). Because \(N\) is the midpoint of \(AB\), triangles \(CBN\) and \(ABC\) have the same altitude to \(AB\) and bases in ratio \(1:2\). Similarly, \(CM=CB/2\) gives
\[
[CMN]=\frac12[CBN]=\frac14[ABC].
\]
Finally, using the common altitude from \(M\) to \(CN\),
\[
n=[OMQ]=\frac{OQ}{CN}[CMN]
=\frac16\cdot\frac14[ABC].
\]
Therefore \(\boxed{[ABC]=24n}\), choice \(\boxed{D}\).

Method 2: Compute a horizontal base and its height

Coordinates provide another route by making \(MP\) horizontal. Choose the unit of length so that \(AB=2\), and place
\[
A=(0,0),\quad B=(2,0),\quad C=(u,v),\qquad v>0.
\]
Here \(u\) is unrestricted, so this placement includes obtuse triangles as well. Choosing a common length scale preserves all area ratios.

The midpoint coordinates are
\[
N=(1,0),\quad
M=\left(\frac{u+2}{2},\frac v2\right),\quad
P=\left(\frac u2,\frac v2\right).
\]
Thus \(MP\) has equation \(y=v/2\). Its intersection with \(CN\) is the midpoint
\[
Q=\left(\frac{u+1}{2},\frac v2\right),
\]
so \(MQ=1/2\).

To find the height of \(O\), write a point on \(AM\) as
\[
(x,y)=\left(\frac{t(u+2)}2,\frac{tv}2\right).
\]
Points on \(CN\) satisfy \(x=1+(u-1)y/v\), where division is valid because \(v>0\). At the intersection, substitution gives
\[
\frac{t(u+2)}2=1+\frac{t(u-1)}2,
\]
so \(3t=2\) and \(y_O=v/3\). The perpendicular distance from \(O\) to the horizontal line \(MQ\) is therefore \(v/2-v/3=v/6\).

It follows that
\[
[OMQ]=\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac v6=\frac v{24},
\qquad
[ABC]=\frac12\cdot2\cdot v=v.
\]
Their area ratio is \(1:24\), so in the original units \(\boxed{[ABC]=24n}\), choice \(\boxed{D}\).
